# Intel AMX and SIMD example study

Collected on 2026-10-13. The source files in this directory are preserved as upstream examples/reference material; none were built or run. `manifest.json` records upstream URLs, immutable Git commits where applicable, byte counts, and SHA-256 digests. `snapshots/` contains the official Intel article pages captured for provenance. The code snapshots are intentionally small: they show selected mechanisms, not complete product libraries.

## What is included

| Local files | Upstream and purpose |
|---|---|
| `amx_intrinsics/test-amxtile.c`, `License.txt`, `README.upstream.md` | Intel’s standalone Linux AMX-TMUL INT8 sample. It is the easiest complete file to follow for tile setup, permission, load, dot product, store, and release. The upstream README says it is a demo, not production code. |
| `intel_optimization_manual/chap20/amx_ref_gemm.hpp`, `amx_preload_gemm.hpp`, `amx_interleaved_gemm.hpp`, `ex4_test.cpp`, `COPYING` | Intel Optimization Reference Manual Chapter 20 examples at the pinned repository commit. The three GEMM headers illustrate successive tile-loop/load-reuse arrangements. They use the manual’s `tile<>`, `tdp`, `tileload`, `tilestore`, and global test fixture names; the small extracted group is for reading, not standalone compilation. `ex4_test.cpp` also refers to files not copied here (`ex1`, `ex3`, and `amx_int8_test_utils.hpp`). |
| `intel_optimization_manual/chap20/bf16_conv.c`, `.h` | Fixed-layout AVX-512 BF16 conversion helper using `_mm512_cvtne2ps_pbh`; this converts two FP32 vectors to packed BF16 and writes a convolution activation buffer. It is not a matrix multiply. |

## Data flow and mechanisms

### AMX tile lifecycle and reuse

`amx_intrinsics/test-amxtile.c` is a signed INT8 × signed INT8 → INT32 example, not BF16. Its input buffers are 16×64 bytes, and the output is 16×16 INT32 (lines 12–16, 93–105, 139–161). `set_tiledata_use()` requests Linux permission for XTILEDATA through `arch_prctl` (lines 71–84); a real application must also check AMX feature support and handle OS/thread permission policy. `init_tile_config()` sets palette 1; tile 0 is configured 16×16 bytes but unused, while tiles 1–3 are 16×64 bytes (lines 29–47). Tile 1’s 64-byte row holds 16 INT32 accumulator columns; tiles 2–3 hold byte operands. It loads the tile config once, loads A/B/C with explicit row stride, runs `_tile_dpbssd`, writes C back, and releases tile state (lines 139–161). It does no blocking, threading, tail handling, or feature dispatch, and its fixed buffers hide those concerns.

The Chapter 20 headers make reuse easier to compare. `amx_ref_gemm.hpp` (lines 20–46) tiles M/N, keeps `M_ACC × N_ACC` accumulator tiles resident through the K loop, loads each B tile per N block, and loads A inside the N loop, so the same A panel can be reloaded for each output-column block. `amx_preload_gemm.hpp` (lines 20–45) loads the A tile set once per K block before iterating N, then reuses it over N accumulators. `amx_interleaved_gemm.hpp` (lines 20–48) likewise keeps A tiles across its N-accumulator loop and uses the `n_acc == 0` guard to avoid reloading A for later N panels. All three retain C accumulators in tile registers across K and store after the reduction (the interleaved example places the final-K store in its inner schedule). Their B tile type is `TILE_K / KPACK` rows by `TILE_N * KPACK` bytes, reflecting a K-packed/VNNI-style RHS layout expected by `tdp`; these snippets assume exact tile-multiple shapes and surrounding definitions.

### BF16 conversion, dot product, and VNNI packing

`bf16_intrinsics/testBF16.cpp` (lines 49–66) loads two 16-float vectors, converts them with `_mm512_cvtne2ps_pbh` into a 32-element BF16 vector, and accumulates paired BF16 products into a 16-lane FP32 accumulator with `_mm512_dpbf16_ps`. `VDPBF16PS` consumes adjacent pairs from each BF16 input and adds the two products to each FP32 lane. The demo uses the same two input vectors for both conversions, has unused `op3_f32`/`v3_f32`, prints a comparison rather than asserting it, and does not cover arbitrary K, tails, or numerical error analysis. It does show the native AVX-512 BF16 instruction flow independently of AMX.

`bf16_conv.c` (lines 20–45) uses `_mm512_cvtne2ps_pbh` for two 16-element FP32 chunks per row and stores the resulting 32 BF16 values; the loop advances through a fixed 16-row scratchpad. It demonstrates conversion/activation-layout movement, not an AMX dot-product kernel.

The Intel manual transpose assembly is shape-specific. The flat-to-flat `.c` wrapper says 64×32 input and 32×64 output, but the upstream `ex22_test.cpp` actually verifies a 64×16 input and 16×64 output. Likewise, the flat-to-VNNI `.c` wrapper says 8×16 → 4×32, while `ex24_test.cpp` tests 64×16 → 8×128 and checks `output[i][2*j + {0,1}] == input[j][2*i + {0,1}]`. These are source-comment/test-shape discrepancies; this study records the tested shapes without asserting why the wrapper comments differ. Both routines use ZMM loads and staged word/dword/qword unpacking; the VNNI lane arrangement groups adjacent K values. They use masks for selected loads but provide no generic arbitrary-dimension API. The `.asm` variants use MASM syntax and Windows argument registers; matching `.s` files are included for GAS/Linux.

oneDNN’s `jit_avx512_core_bf16cvt.hpp` shows two complementary ideas. It emits native `vcvtneps2bf16` when AVX-512 BF16 is available and otherwise uses a bit-level emulation sequence with rounding and special-value handling (`bf16_emulation_t`, lines 49–142; dispatch at lines 195–216). Its reorder JIT gathers two 16-channel halves into `[s][16c][2s]` via `vpermw` and a permutation table, processing full vectors and then a masked tail (lines 294–386). This is a packing/reorder helper, not the project’s residual decomposition routine.

### AVX2/AVX-512 vector work and tails

`MatrixMultiplication.cpp` uses unaligned YMM/ZMM loads and FMA to compute a dot product per row, then horizontally reduces each accumulator (AVX2 at lines 60–74; AVX-512 at lines 77–89). It has no matrix tiling or reuse across a second output dimension. It initializes a scalar result but only times AVX2 and AVX-512, uses Windows `RDTSC`, and runs each 100,000 times in a fixed order (lines 20, 26, 131–168); do not use its printed ratio as a controlled architecture benchmark.

`MandelbrotImage.cpp` uses vector comparisons to form AVX2 masks and AVX-512 `__mmask16` masks while iterating multiple complex points (AVX2 at lines 36–54; AVX-512 at lines 87–105). This illustrates per-lane work masks, not a memory-tail mask: both image loops step by the vector width and assume divisibility. Its comparison loop checks only the first pixel of each 16-pixel block (lines 150–156), so the sanity check does not validate every lane. It also uses Windows `RDTSC` and fixed dimensions for demonstration.

The Chapter 18 `avx512_vector_dp.s` is the FP64 SIMD example in this selection. It merges two sparse index streams, compares 8 indices from each side, uses `vpconflictd` plus permutation controls to identify pairs with equal indices, loads their double values, and accumulates products with `vfmadd231pd`; a scalar tail handles remaining entries (vector loop at lines 63–120; scalar tail at 130–168). Correctness requires each index stream to be sorted, inferred from the monotone merge advancement; the wrapper only checks non-null buffers and `max_els >= 8` (`avx512_vector_dp.c`). The scalar reference handles the same intersection. This is an irregular sparse kernel, not dense GEMM; it requires AVX-512 conflict-detection support, lacks arbitrary unsorted-index handling, and uses a different reduction order from the scalar loop. `transpose_avx512.s` uses a fixed 64-entry permutation mask and `vpermi2w` to transpose 50 contiguous 8×8 `uint16_t` matrices; its wrapper documents 64-byte alignment and the exact batch shape. The code illustrates SIMD shuffle/permutation and alignment contracts, not general transpose tails.

### Mature JIT GEMM and copy path

In `onednn_x64/jit_avx512_core_amx_gemm_kern.cpp`, `generate()` builds machine code through Xbyak, choosing instruction type and unroll sizes from operand/output type (lines 62–101). For BF16-to-FP32, `typec == 0` selects the BF16 kernel type and a K unroll of two; the code maintains four output accumulator tiles arranged as a 2×2 block (`tmm4`–`tmm7`) and loads/reuses two A and two B tiles across the K loop (lines 292–411). It conditionally uses `tilezero` or loads existing C according to beta, programs tile dimensions as M/N tails change, caches the current tile config, and omits inactive tiles at edges (lines 197–289, 300–330). K/M/N blocking and packed input panels are expected to be supplied by the surrounding GEMM/copy pipeline. This is a JIT microkernel generator, not an end-to-end API call.

`jit_avx512_core_amx_copy_kern.cpp` contains distinct non-transposed/transposed A/B packing paths (`kernel_AN/BN/AT/BT`, lines 141–300), vector shuffle/unpack stages, and masked edge handling. Its outer loops break dimensions into unrolled blocks, derive masks from remainders, and zero-fill missing loads (lines 302–478). This is the strongest reference here for separating layout conversion from the compute microkernel; its mask/corner logic is more general than the fixed-size Intel manual assembly.

The oneDNN excerpts contain no thread-team or NUMA first-touch policy: those belong to higher-level primitive scheduling and memory allocation paths that were intentionally not copied. The code also depends on oneDNN/Xbyak internals and cannot be validated in isolation from those dependencies.

## Relation to this repository

The project kernel in `/home/caiweili/ozAMX/src/gemm.cpp` uses 256×256×256 outer blocks and 32×32×32 AMX microtiles (line 21), explicitly packs two-slice BF16 panels and stores B in adjacent-K pair order (`bpanel_index`, lines 166–171 and packing loops 197–205). The native BF16 tile kernel accumulates a 2×2 group of output tiles (`_tile_dpbf16ps`, lines 258–278), similar in broad structure to oneDNN’s 2×2 AMX output tile. The project’s distinctive numerical work is direct FP32-to-BF16 residual construction (lines 32–75), FP64 residual construction (lines 102–121), and FP64 emulation by accumulating AMX FP32 component products into a double block (lines 453–484); the samples above are not a correctness proof for those algorithms.

Useful transfers are: retain output accumulators across K; reuse a loaded A tile across multiple N tiles; make RHS pair layout explicit; keep packing/transposition a separately measured phase; handle both compute masks and memory-tail masks; and dispatch/emulate conversion based on ISA support. The external samples do not imply that this project’s accuracy, performance, or arbitrary-dimension behavior is correct. The manual GEMM headers and transpose routines are fixed-shape examples; the AMX intrinsic sample is INT8; and oneDNN’s API-level setup, dispatch, threading, and NUMA behavior are outside the copied excerpts.

## Provenance and caveats

- Intel AMX-TMUL source is pinned to `intel/AMX-TMUL-Code-Samples` commit `e4029b9184bac98ecb0c4472bc883bccc190933b`; the upstream README identifies it as MIT and demo-only.
- Optimization Manual examples are pinned to `intel/optimization-manual` tag commit `5cd28bc054b30a3a0926484dedb8d0fdc35b3879`. The copied files retain Intel’s permissive per-file notice; `COPYING` is kept from that exact commit.
- The Chapter 18 AVX-512 samples are from the same pinned manual commit. Their `.s` files are Linux/GAS assembly; the `.c` files are the argument-check wrappers. The headers, scalar/vector test harness, and remaining full-project files are not included.
- The manual repository README describes the complete upstream project as buildable examples with unit tests and documents per-example assumptions/wrappers. This study intentionally carries only the selected files, so `ex4_test.cpp` has missing fixture includes and none of these extracts is promised to build by itself.
- AVX-512 blog code is pinned to archived repository commit `5e3db2ec738bafb363b754b2eb1c5ac197d37cfe`. Individual code files identify Intel and SPDX MIT; the upstream README says the project is discontinued.
- oneDNN is pinned to commit `1bd572dd2b2efcac7de788c91c6096ccb30f8e4e`; its Apache-2.0 `LICENSE` is included. The three selected source files depend on broader oneDNN headers and Xbyak.
- Intel’s BF16 article page labels its linked sample “3-Clause BSD License”, but the downloaded ZIP’s `License.txt` is MIT-style text and `testBF16.cpp` says SPDX MIT. Both the page snapshot and original ZIP are preserved; this study does not resolve the discrepancy.
- The AVX-512 blog examples use Windows headers and timer APIs. The manual’s `.asm` and `.s` assembly variants are toolchain-specific alternatives. Do not infer full application portability or Xeon 8454H performance from source alone.
- No performance measurements, builds, or execution were performed on these collected references.
